newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-LARGER BUNKERS WOULD CONTAIN WOODS, SAYS FALDO.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LARGER BUNKERS WOULD CONTAIN WOODS, SAYS FALDO.

text.p: Nick Faldo called on Wednesday for golf course designers to create larger bunkers to contain the threat posed by the huge hitting of Tiger Woods.
In England to play in this week's British PGA championship, the former world number one said Woods had an enormous advantage because of his power off the tee.
"He's got the game throttled. He's playing a different golf course to the rest of us," said Faldo, who is now based on the U.S. Tour.

But Faldo said Woods, who followed his record 12-stroke U.S. Masters triumph last month by adding the Byron Nelson Classic on Sunday for his fifth win as a professional, could be contained if bunkers were larger.
"At the present time if there is a bunker 240 yards out, the rest of us have to play to avoid it. But he can blow his drive right over it.
"That gives him an extra 70 or 80 yards of fairway to hit to.
"But if the bunker were extended to cover distance from 240 yards to 320 yards, then he would have to hit it to the right place like all of us."
Faldo said the first hole at Augusta was a prime example.
"With the bunker on the right, we all have to play to the left. Not him because he just flies the bunker.
"He's aiming at a fairway twice as wide as I'm aiming at," said Faldo, who missed the halfway cut at Augusta.
Woods averaged about 325 yards with his drives at Augusta.
"It's amazing to think that one man has come along and they are thinking of changing some very historic golf courses," Faldo said.
"His driver and his putter are his key clubs but his length is the thing. Golf course designers have got to cater for that.
"But good luck to him," Faldo added in admiration. "He is a player for the '90s. He is making a major contribution to the way the U.S. Tour is going now."
Faldo, winner of the Masters three times, felt he could have won the fabled Grand Slam in 1990 when he captured both the Masters and the British Open.
"I lipped out at a crucial hole at the U.S. Open," he said. He tied for third there, then after his British Open victory he tied for 19th at the U.S. PGA.
"When I was hot, I was about 100-1 with the bookmakers against doing the slam. Tiger must be half that."

Faldo felt the Congressional Course near Washington, where the U.S. Open will be played next month, could be good for Woods. But his big problem could be at Royal Troon, venue of the British Open in July.
"If a good old gale blows and the fairways are rock hard, it would be tough for him."
